idiom_name: version column with a conditional UPDATE through the database client
implementation_notes: The classic structure is hand-written over whichever database client the project uses: read the version with the row, bind it into WHERE id = ? AND version = ? on the write, and test the affected-row count (PQcmdTuples or sqlite3_changes) to decide whether the copy was stale - no standard-library facility supplies persistence, so there is nothing to replace it with. For a shared in-process record the token becomes std::atomic<uint64_t> and the check is compare_exchange_strong against the value the caller read (C++11), which is the same contract with the CPU as arbiter. Keep the SQL form when the store must be the arbiter and the atomic form for lock-free shared state; the classic hand-written structure stays justified because neither the language nor its standard library ships a mapper.
pitfalls: compare_exchange_strong overwrites the expected operand on failure - that variable no longer holds 'the version I read', so a retry loop must reset it from the freshly observed value.
A default-constructed std::atomic is not initialised before C++20; a token read from uninitialised storage compares against garbage.
Copying a versioned struct by value splits the token from the store that arbitrates it; only the authoritative copy may be compared.

variants.name: In-process atomic version token (compare-exchange loop)
variants.implementation_notes: When the shared resource is memory rather than a database, the per-record token is a std::atomic holding the version the writer last saw: compare_exchange_strong(expected, expected + 1) succeeds only if nothing changed in between, and on failure rewrites expected with the observed token so the caller can re-read and retry. It is the same detect-then-retry contract with the CPU as arbiter, and it replaces the SQL predicate for lock-free shared state - not for durable data, where the store must remain the arbiter. Use it where contention is bounded and the retry loop can be, because a CAS loop has no queueing fairness.
pitfalls: A CAS only guards the token; the payload must be published through a pointer with matching release/acquire ordering or readers can still observe torn data.
Lock-free retry loops can livelock under contention - bound the attempts and fall back to a mutex.
